questions.question: What property makes a VDF different from a regular hash function?
options: A VDF requires a minimum sequential computation time that cannot be parallelised
A VDF is faster to compute than to verify
A VDF output is unpredictable even after the input is known
A VDF uses a secret key that only the verifier knows
questions.explanation: The defining property of a VDF is sequentiality: T steps cannot be parallelised, enforcing a minimum wall-clock delay regardless of how many cores an attacker uses.

questions.question: In the RSA-group VDF y = x^(2^T) mod N, why is the group of unknown order important?
options: Without knowing φ(N), an attacker cannot shortcut 2^T squarings to fewer operations
An unknown group order prevents the verifier from checking the proof
It ensures that x and N are always coprime
It makes the modular squaring operation constant-time
questions.explanation: Knowing φ(N) = (p-1)(q-1) lets you reduce the exponent 2^T mod φ(N) and evaluate the VDF in O(log T) work. Unknown order closes this shortcut.

questions.question: In the Wesolowski proof, what is π (pi)?
options: π = x^(floor(2^T / l)) mod N, where l is the hash-derived challenge
π = y^l mod N, a commitment to the output
π = H(x || y || T), the challenge itself
π = x^(2^T mod l) mod N, the residual squaring
questions.explanation: The prover computes q = floor(2^T / l) and sets π = x^q mod N. Verification then checks π^l * x^r == y where r = 2^T mod l.

questions.question: How does the Wesolowski verifier check the proof without redoing all T squarings?
options: It checks (π^l * x^r) mod N == y, where r = 2^T mod l
It checks π^(2^T) mod N == y directly
It re-runs T/2 squarings and compares with π
It checks H(π || l) == y
questions.explanation: The verification equation π^l * x^r == y follows from the definition of π = x^q and the identity 2^T = q*l + r. The verifier only needs two modular exponentiations.

questions.question: What attack does trapdoor-free RSA modulus generation prevent?
options: An attacker who knows p and q can compute φ(N) and shortcut the VDF evaluation
An attacker can forge Wesolowski proofs without knowing x
An attacker can recover x from y using the discrete logarithm
An attacker can parallelise the T squarings across many cores
questions.explanation: Knowing p and q gives φ(N), which allows reducing 2^T mod φ(N) and computing y in O(log T) work. Discarding p and q after generating N prevents this.

questions.question: In a VDF-based time-lock encryption scheme, what is published alongside the ciphertext?
options: The puzzle input x and the delay T (but not y or the key)
The VDF output y encrypted with the public key
The Wesolowski proof π so anyone can decrypt immediately
A commitment to y using a hash function
questions.explanation: Publishing x and T lets anyone solve the puzzle to derive y = VDF(x, T, N) and then decrypt. Publishing y directly would bypass the delay entirely.

questions.question: Why should the input x to a time-lock puzzle be derived from a future-committed nonce?
options: To prevent the puzzle creator from pre-computing y before publishing the ciphertext
To ensure x is always smaller than N
To make the Wesolowski challenge l unpredictable
To guarantee gcd(x, N) == 1
questions.explanation: If the creator can choose x freely they can run the VDF privately before announcing the puzzle, learning y (and hence the decryption key) before the intended delay expires.

questions.question: What is the main limitation of the toy VDF implemented in this lesson compared to production systems like Chiavdf?
options: The 92-bit RSA modulus is easily factorable, making the group order known and the delay bypassable
The Wesolowski proof is incorrect and always returns pi = 1
Repeated squaring cannot be parallelised even in this implementation
The SHA-256 challenge hash is not collision-resistant enough for VDF use
questions.explanation: With a 92-bit modulus, an attacker can factor N in seconds using standard tools, learn φ(N), and shortcut all T squarings. Production VDFs use ≥1024-bit moduli with trapdoor-free setup.
